quiz.q: What are the two main things Rust is designed to give you at the same time?
options: A garbage collector and dynamic typing
quiz.explain: Rust's whole pitch is programs that are both fast and free of memory bugs, achieved without a garbage collector.

quiz.q: How does Rust manage memory safety?
options: A background garbage collector cleans up while the program runs
You call free() by hand like in C
The compiler checks ownership rules before the program runs and rejects unsafe code
It never frees memory, so programs leak
quiz.explain: Rust has no garbage collector and no manual free(). The compiler enforces ownership rules at compile time, refusing to build unsafe code.

quiz.q: Which single concept is described as the core idea that makes the rest of Rust click?
quiz.explain: Ownership is Rust's rule for who is responsible for each value and when it's cleaned up. It's the heart of the language.

quiz.q: For a beginner, which topics should you save for later rather than start with?
quiz.explain: Macros, unsafe, and async are advanced. Beginners should orient first, then learn basics and ownership before touching them.

flashcards.front: What two qualities does Rust aim to deliver together?
flashcards.back: Speed (like C/C++) and memory safety (like garbage-collected languages) — with no garbage collector.

flashcards.front: When does Rust check that your memory use is safe?
flashcards.back: At compile time. The compiler enforces ownership rules before the program ever runs and refuses to build unsafe code.

flashcards.front: What does 'Rust is explicit by default' mean?
flashcards.back: Rust rarely does hidden things behind your back; you say what you mean, so code tells you the truth about what it does.

flashcards.front: What is the one big idea to learn slowly, because it makes the rest of Rust make sense?
flashcards.back: Ownership — who owns each value and when it gets cleaned up.
